headlines.title: 1 dead following multi-vehicle crash on I-80 in Berkeley
headlines.description: A deadly crash involving multiple vehicles on Interstate 80 in Berkeley is under investigation, according to the California Highway Patrol. The collision was reported just before 3:30 p.m. Friday and shut down several lanes on westbound I-80 near the University Avenue exit. At least five vehicles were involved in the collision and one person was pronounced dead at the scene, CHP said. There was no estimated time lanes would reopen and motorists were encouraged to use alternate routes. headlines.title: Man, woman dead after shooting at Oakland Hills home
headlines.description: A 61-year-old man and 63-year-old woman were found dead from apparent gunshot wounds outside their Oakland Hills home late Friday morning, according to police. Oakland and Berkeley police officers responded at about 10:45 a.m. to 499 Panoramic Way, not far from the University of California, Berkeley campus, to investigate reported gunshots, Oakland Police Department Assistant Chief Casey Johnson said. Officers found the man and woman suffering from apparent gunshot wounds outside the home. They both died at the scene, Johnson said. The man and woman appeared to be married and were residents at the home, according to Johnson. A firearm was recovered at the scene, Johnson said. It wasn’t immediately known if the shooting was a homicide or murder-suicide. “Everything’s a possibility until we can fully investigate this incident,” Johnson said. Johnson said there was no one in custody as of 1:30 p.m., adding that police were not looking for anyone at-large and that there was no threat to the surrounding neighborhood.

headlines.title: Padilla pays unannounced visit to SFO's immigration holding facility
headlines.description: Sen. Alex Padilla of California made an impromptu visit to San Francisco International Airport’s immigration holding facility Thursday night in response to constituents’ concerns that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has been using the facility more frequently in recent months at the direction of the Trump administration. Padilla said his visit to the Customs and Border Protection holding facility was part of an effort to achieve some transparency regarding increased operations by ICE agents at SFO. Padilla said he was greeted by a few uniformed Customs and Border Protection officers who ultimately toured him through the customs inspection areas. Padilla said there were less than 10 people at the immigration holding facility, but he did not know why they were there nor how long they had been there. Padilla said the holding area should not be used as a formal ICE facility. “There are certain standards that need to be met, and they’re sort of makeshift, trying to comply with,” Padilla said. “Not just access to restrooms and drinking water and food, but things like accommodations for folks that are being detained there to be able to communicate with their family or to communicate with their lawyer.” Concerns have been raised by immigration attorneys and family members over some people being held for days. In a statement, a Customs and Border Protection spokesperson said the facilities at SFO offer appropriate accommodations, including access to medical services, if needed. “As part of the inspection process, certain travelers may require additional processing based on the circumstances of their case,” the statement read. “The length and nature of that processing can vary depending on a number of factors…” There has been increased attention on SFO’s immigration holding facility after two high-profile incidents this year in which ICE agents detained two different women who were traveling through the airport. NBC News reported that immigration agents in August increased the number of arrests and detentions at airports across the country. Padilla said visits like the one he made are part of a coordinated effort among some of his Democratic congressional colleagues to ensure the issue stays in the spotlight. “Because our Republican colleagues in Congress – they’re the majority – refuse to hold hearings in committee, to demand more information and answers from this administration,” Padilla said.

headlines.title: 49ers owner Jed York suspended for 6 games after his arrest in prostitution sting
headlines.description: The NFL suspended San Francisco 49ers owner Jed York for six games Friday following his arrest earlier this year in a prostitution sting in Ohio. The league announced that York also was fined $500,000 for violating the league’s personal conduct policy. York has not attended any games or league meetings so far this season and was credited with three games served. He is eligible to return on Oct. 20, following the team’s game the previous night against Washington. The NFL’s fall league meetings begin that day in New York. York said in a statement released by the team that he accepts the punishment given by the league and apologized for his actions. “To my family, to the players, coaches, and employees of the San Francisco 49ers, to our fans and partners, I am deeply sorry,” he said. “This was an inexcusable mistake and I take full responsibility. What I did does not reflect my values or the man I strive to be for my family. While I fell short of the model I want to set for my sons, I now hope to show them the importance of owning up to one’s failures, and that even our worst moments teach us to be better. Leading the 49ers is a privilege, and one I don’t take lightly. Your trust will have to be earned back over time, and I look forward to that work ahead.” York was arrested in a mobile home park by the Mahoning Valley Human Trafficking Task Force in August after police said he was attempting to pay $160 for sex with a woman he believed to be a prostitute. York was booked into jail and was released after posting a $5,000 bond. York was initially charged with engaging in prostitution, but prosecutors amended that to disorderly conduct. He pleaded no contest to that charge and to possessing criminal tools for using his phone to respond to an undercover online prostitution advertisement. He was sentenced to one day in jail for both offenses to be served concurrently and was credited with one day served when he pleaded no contest. He also was fined $1,150. Police seized the $160 from York and that was later given to the human trafficking task force as part of the plea. York also completed an online course. Owners have been previously punished for violating the personal conduct policy. The late Indianapolis Colts owner Jim Irsay was suspended for six games and fined $500,000 following a guilty plea to driving while impaired in 2014. New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft was investigated but not punished by the league after he was arrested in Florida in 2019 for allegedly paying for sex with a woman at a massage parlor. The charge was later dropped after a court ruled that police violated the rights of Kraft and the other customers when they secretly installed video cameras inside massage rooms at the spa. York spent most of the summer in Ohio, where he grew up near Youngstown and had been away from the team even before his arrest. He had filed for divorce from his wife, Danielle, in May, according to court records. York took over day-to-day control of the 49ers from his parents in 2008. He became the team’s principal owner in 2024. After some initial struggles under York’s leadership, the team has been a consistent contender since hiring coach Kyle Shanahan and general manager John Lynch in 2017. The Niners have made the Super Bowl three times under York’s leadership, losing in the 2012 season under coach Jim Harbaugh and the 2019 and ’23 seasons under Shanahan and Lynch. York also oversaw the building of Levi’s Stadium in Santa Clara. The team moved from San Francisco to the new stadium in 2014. The stadium has hosted two Super Bowls, a World Cup and a College Football Playoff title game.

headlines.title: New museum tells the story of Dogpatch's industrial past
headlines.description: As San Francisco’s Dogpatch neighborhood undergoes a metamorphosis from gritty industrial hub to hip cutting-edge neighborhood, a new museum has popped up to remind the neighborhood of its past. The Pier 70 Time Machine sits tucked away on the second floor of newly restored Building 12 at Pier 70, where legions of workers once built Navy destroyers during World War II — but now houses a scooter business, padel courts, a brewery and other businesses. The museum was opened by Peter Linenthal and Bill Perez, two historians who merged their collections of ephemera to tell the history of the area’s shipbuilding along with the stories of nearby neighborhoods of Potrero Hill, Mission Bay and the now-gone Irish Hill. “People don’t know that where we are in Dogpatch was an industrial hub that shortly after the founding of San Francisco, that really built the city that we know today,” said Linenthal, who runs the Potrero Archives Project. The 4,000-square-foot museum is filled with pieces of industrial past, such as a room devoted to the tools used in shipbuilding. Perez, who once worked in Bethlehem Steel — the massive shipbuilding operation that supplied military ships during World War II — is now president of the Bethlehem Shipyard Museum. Before opening the new museum, his collection of industrial items filled his garage. Similarly, Linenthal stored his collection of items telling the stories of the nearby neighborhoods, with hopes of one day having a place to show it all. “It’s really a dream come true to have a space like this where we can share our collections for free with the public,” Linenthal said. Linenthal pointed out an old-time dentist chair that once belonged to Potrero Hill dentist Dr. Jean Pierre Cantou, who operated in the neighborhood between the 1930s and the 1960s. Nearby sat a replica of a tule boat that would’ve been used by Ramaytush Ohlone indigenous tribes that once inhabited Potrero Point more than 1,000 years before the arrival of the gold miners. Linenthal pointed out a large, glowing-red beacon that once sat atop a huge gas tank located near present-day Pennsylvania and Cesar Chavez streets. “We’re telling the stories of the people that worked in those industries, in the development of those industries,” said Linenthal. “And actually we’re going back to tell the story of the native people who lived here thousands of years ago.” Admission to the museum is free — it’s open Fridays from 5 p.m. to 8 p.m. and Saturdays from noon to 4 p.m. The museum’s founders plan to expand their offerings to include more interactive exhibits to further interest young people in the neighborhood’s many stories. “One of our goals is to become a cultural hub,” said Perez. The museum also tells the story of Wendy the Welder, a counterpart to the famous Rosie the Riveter icon that paid tribute to women who worked in the shipyards. Another exhibit pays tribute to Irish Hill, the one-time working-class neighborhood that existed on a nearby hill that is no longer there. As Dogpatch and the Pier 70 area undergo a massive revamp, Linenthal hopes the museum will inform people of the origins of the brick buildings and metal barns that once were home base to a thriving industrial machine. “Things are changing so quickly that I think it’s important to look at the past just to understand all the changes the city has been through before,” Linenthal said.

headlines.title: Steve Hilton faces steep odds in bid for California governor after 20-year GOP drought
headlines.description: To become California’s next governor, Republican Steve Hilton must conjure up a feat of political wizardry, the equivalent of pulling voters out of thin air in a state that hasn’t elected a Republican to any statewide office in two decades. “I’ve never said it’s going to be easy,” Hilton said in an interview with The Associated Press. “It’s obviously an uphill battle. I still see this as a winnable race.” With mail ballots scheduled to arrive at homes in early October, the former Fox News commentator is angling to pull off what would be one of the great upsets in California record books against Democrat Xavier Becerra. Aligned against him in the heavily Democratic state are the weight of recent history, a national electorate that has soured on President Donald Trump and, perhaps inescapably, basic math. Any Republican starts at a disadvantage. Registered Democrats outnumber Republicans by a staggering 4.6 million voters, a margin approaching 2-to-1 statewide. Trump — who has endorsed Hilton’s candidacy — is widely loathed outside his conservative base in a state the president often depicts as representing all that is wrong in America. “I like Steve a lot, but the math is very hard,” says GOP consultant Mike Murphy, who advised the last Republican to hold the office, former Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger. He was elected to his second term in 2006. “I think the most relevant equation is how many cases of beer you have to drink to be drunk enough to think it’s doable in this election cycle with the Trump dynamic and the registration advantage the Democrats have,” Murphy wrote in an email. “My model starts at four cases.” California Sep 30 Decision 2026 Sep 29 A Democratic reckoning that has never come For years, Republicans envisioned that one day the state’s Democratic ribs would crack, as voters faithful to the brand grew weary of wallet-sapping taxes, the nation’s top gas prices, an unchecked homeless crisis and home prices and rents that drain family budgets. “We will win because the argument for change is irresistible,” the Britain-born Hilton says. To defeat Becerra, Hilton will need to upend what has become a familiar pattern in California general elections. Frequently, Democratic statewide candidates pull in roughly 60% of the vote on Election Day. Rival Republicans, around 40%. Part of Hilton’s challenge is overcoming the baked-in notion that California’s political DNA is immutable. “We just need to overcome the sense that after 20 years of one party running everything, it is actually possible to get change. That’s the biggest thing I think we’re fighting against,” Hilton said. He repeated that message again during a Wednesday debate on CNN, the only television matchup scheduled for the general election. In his pursuit of a breakthrough, Hilton has anchored his campaign to making California more affordable, including bringing gas prices down to $3 a gallon. Yet he doesn’t appear to be gaining the traction he needs to catch the Democrat. A September poll conducted by the University of California, Berkeley, Institute of Governmental Studies found that Becerra had a sizable lead over Hilton. Some of his proposals are clearly crafted to snag voters’ attention, even if it is not clear how some would clear a Democratic-controlled legislature or other regulatory hurdles. Among them: cut in half residents’ utility bills, now among the nation’s highest; eliminate state income taxes on the first $150,000 in earnings; and abolish the much-maligned Department of Motor Vehicles. He believes about a quarter of the vote is up for grabs, including people who have voted for Democrats but aren’t rigidly faithful to the party — largely working-class voters and those without a college education. He sees room to pick up more votes among Latinos and women, too. And he will need a heroic turnout from Republicans. At the same time, he has been campaigning in the Los Angeles area — the state’s Democratic nucleus, where statewide elections can be won or lost depending on turnout. Becerra argues that Hilton will be little more than another loyalist for the Trump administration, imposing the president’s conservative agenda in California. Fewer competitive races in a polarized nation The number of truly competitive races nationwide has dwindled as many states veer to the political left or right. Up until the late 1980s, California was for many years a reliable win for the GOP in presidential elections. But a growing immigrant population and a shifting economy — including the collapse of the defense industry and the rise of Silicon Valley — transformed the state and its voting patterns. Bedrock issues that define the California electorate — including widespread support for abortion rights and environmental protection — could make it difficult for some voters to consider backing a GOP candidate, especially in the Trump era. After months of turmoil with a large field in the June primary election, the contest to succeed the outgoing Newsom has settled into a stolid affair. With numbers on his side, Becerra’s low-key campaign is an acknowledgment that if he avoids mistakes, he is likely to get the job. Still, polling conducted in early September by the Public Policy Institute of California found about half of voters think the state is moving in the wrong direction while a majority think economic conditions will be bad over the next year. California — where Democrats hold every statewide office and dominate the legislature — has one of the nation’s highest unemployment rates. Its gas prices are the highest in the nation, and its utility prices near the top nationally. Home prices often soar into the seven digits. After decades of meteoric growth, the population has essentially flatlined, with California expected to lose a congressional seat as states like Florida and Texas grow at a faster pace. One Republican who got close in recent years is Lanhee Chen, who picked up nearly 45% of the vote in his 2022 race for state controller. For Hilton to be successful “he has to turn it into a referendum on one-party governance,” Chen said.
headlines.source: Michael R. Blood | The Associated Press

headlines.title: ‘Zoo Lights' return to San Francisco Zoo after hiatus
headlines.description: After nearly a decade, holiday magic is returning to the San Francisco Zoo. “Zoo Lights” will officially return next month after ending its run in 2018. The holiday favorite transforms the zoo into a nighttime winter wonderland with more than 1 million twinkling lights. The event will also feature a massive frozen forest, animatronic dinosaurs and nods to San Francisco icons such as the Golden Gate Bridge and cable cars. Zoo Lights runs from Nov. 6 through Jan. 3. Tickets go on sale soon at sfzoo.org.

headlines.title: Driver arrested after alleged hit-and-run collision with pedestrian in San Francisco
headlines.description: A man was arrested after an alleged hit-and-run collision in San Francisco that left a pedestrian with life-threatening injuries Thursday evening, according to police. The collision was reported at about 7:05 p.m. in the area of Moscow Street and France Avenue near the Crocker Amazon Playground. San Francisco police said a truck driver hit a 43-year-old man in a crosswalk. The driver was later arrested on suspicion of hit and run. An update on the pedestrian’s condition was not immediately available Friday morning. Anyone with information about the case is asked to call the SFPD tip line at 415-575-4444 or to send a tip by text message to TIP411 with SFPD at the start of the message.

headlines.title: Hardly Strictly Bluegrass Festival kicks off in San Francisco
headlines.description: The 25th Hardly Strictly Bluegrass Festival kicks off Friday at the Golden Gate Park in San Francisco, with large crowds already arriving for opening day. The free festival runs through Sunday. This year’s event includes 15 performers who will weave Dolly Parton themes into their concerts. Among the featured performers is Robert Plant, the legendary singer and original member of Led Zeppelin. Emmylou Harris is also among the artists in this year’s lineup. The Dolly Parton tributes hold special meaning for longtime Hardly Strictly fans who wish they could have seen her performance at the festival 21 years ago. NBC Bay Area’s Thom Jensen has the full report in the video above.

headlines.title: North Bay DUI stop takes unexpected turn when driver's mom also gets arrested
headlines.description: A Cotati DUI stop took an unexpected turn earlier this week when the driver’s mother showed up to pick up her son’s dog and vehicle – and officers ended up arresting her, too. A Cotati officer was patrolling downtown Wednesday when a passerby flagged him down and reported a driver up ahead who appeared to be drunk, according to the Cotati Police Department on social media. The officer caught up with the vehicle and allegedly saw multiple traffic violations that were consistent with impairment. After stopping the vehicle, the officer conducted a DUI investigation that resulted in the driver being arrested on suspicion of driving under the combined influence of alcohol and drugs. The driver then asked officers to call his mother so she could come pick up his dog and vehicle. “At the request of the suspect, the suspect’s mother was contacted to respond out to the scene and retrieve his dog and his vehicle – and was specifically asked over the phone if she herself had been drinking,” the department said. “She said she had not.” But when the mother arrived, officers allegedly saw multiple signs that she was intoxicated. A second DUI investigation followed, and she was arrested. The mother later provided a chemical test showing a blood alcohol level of 0.18%, according to police. Her son refused a chemical test, but his blood was eventually drawn under a warrant. Both were booked into the Sonoma County Jail. “This is another great example of how utilizing ride share services, planning ahead, or just not making the decision to get behind the wheel after drinking would have prevented all of this,” the department said.

headlines.title: Guy Fieri to tape ‘Tournament of Champions' in Sonoma County
headlines.description: Celebrity chef and Sonoma County resident Guy Fieri will tape the new season of his show “Tournament of Champions” this month in Windsor. The show pits 32 chefs against each other in a single-elimination, sudden-death tournament. Tapings will take place during the mornings and afternoons from Oct. 8 to Oct. 23. Audience members must be at least 18 years old. Tickets can be requested through on-camera-audiences.com.
